distinctions.note: Annoy is neutral and mild, suitable for any setting, while 'piss off' is vulgar and much stronger.
Upset often describes sadness or hurt feelings, whereas 'piss off' describes irritation or anger.

collocations: don't piss off the wrong person

examples.everyday: Stop tapping your pen during the movie, you're really pissing me off.
examples.professional: Don't send that email yet, it could piss off the legal team.
examples.analytical: Thinkers who challenge comfortable assumptions often piss off the people who benefit from those assumptions.

nuance.analogy: Like a match tossed onto a pile of dry paper: a small remark can flare into anger.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English pissen, from Old French pissier, from Vulgar Latin pissiare, probably imitative.
common_mistakes: Putting the object in the wrong place: say 'piss me off' or 'piss off my boss', not 'piss off me'.
Using it in formal writing or at work, where it sounds crude and unprofessional.
Confusing the imperative 'Piss off!' (Go away!) with the milder phrasal verb meaning 'annoy'.

senses.definition: A stop-motion technique where live actors are used as a frame-by-frame subject in an animated film, by repeatedly posing while one or more frame is taken and changing pose slightly before the next frame or frames.
senses.example: The student film used pixilation, with actors freezing mid-step for every single frame.

core.definition: A stop-motion film technique in which live actors are photographed frame by frame, posing slightly differently each time so they appear to move unnaturally.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -LAY-, the third syllable. The x is /ks/, and the ending is -shun, not -tion as in 'nation'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a specialized term in film and animation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in film schools, animation studies and film criticism, rarely in everyday talk. It is a different word from pixelation, which refers to digital image blocks. If you want the everyday idea, say stop-motion animation with real people.

distinctions.note: Pixelation means visible square blocks in a digital image; pixilation is a film technique with live actors posed frame by frame.
Stop-motion is the general category, often using puppets or clay; pixilation specifically uses live human performers.

examples.everyday: Last night we watched a short film where people freeze in odd poses, and my friend said it was pixilation.
examples.professional: For the commercial we can use pixilation with the actual staff instead of building CGI characters.
examples.analytical: Pixilation makes the performer's body into an animated object, so the film questions where the human ends and the mechanical begins.

nuance.analogy: Like a flipbook made of real people, where each page catches someone in a slightly different pose.
nuance.etymology: Formed from pixilated, itself from pixie; the film sense is a later extension of the older 'bewitched' meaning.
common_mistakes: Confusing pixilation with pixelation, which is a digital term.
Stressing the wrong syllable; the stress is on -LAY-, not on the first syllable.

senses.definition: An area; somewhere within an area.
senses.example: They live at Westminster Place.

senses.definition: An open space, particularly a city square, market square, or courtyard.
A street, sometimes but not always surrounding a public place, square, or plaza of the same name.
senses.example: They live at Westminster Place.

senses.definition: An inhabited area: a village, town, or city.
Any area of the earth: a region.
senses.example: He is going back to his native place on vacation.

senses.definition: The area one occupies, particularly somewhere to sit.
senses.example: We asked the restaurant to give us a table with three places.

senses.definition: The area where one lives: one's home, formerly country estates and farms.
senses.example: Do you want to come over to my place later?

senses.definition: An area of the body, especially the skin.
senses.example: Which place hurts the most?

senses.definition: A location or position in space.
senses.example: I'll check places I think she might be.

senses.definition: Proper or usual position.
senses.example: A place for everything, and everything in its place.

senses.definition: A particular location in a book or document, particularly the current location of a reader.
senses.example: I lost my place when you interrupted me.

senses.definition: A state of mind.
senses.example: I'm in a strange place at the moment.

senses.definition: A responsibility or position in an organization.
senses.example: It is really not my place to say what is right and wrong in this case.

senses.definition: A role or purpose; a station.
senses.example: It is really not my place to say what is right and wrong in this case.

senses.definition: The position as a member of a sports team.
senses.example: He lost his place in the national team.

senses.definition: The position of a contestant at the close of a competition.
senses.example: We thought we would win but only ended up in fourth place.

senses.definition: The position of first, second, or third at the finish, especially the second position.
senses.example: to win a bet on a horse for place

senses.definition: Numerically, the column counting a certain quantity.
senses.example: three decimal places; the hundreds place

senses.definition: Ordinal relation; position in the order of proceeding.
senses.example: That's what I said in the first place!

senses.definition: Reception; effect, implying the making room for.
(dated) An area to urinate and defecate: an outhouse or lavatory.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To put (someone or something) in a specific location.
senses.example: He placed the glass on the table.

senses.definition: To earn a given spot in a competition; to rank at a certain position.
senses.example: The Cowboys placed third in the league.

senses.definition: To finish second, especially of horses or dogs.
senses.example: In the third race: Aces Up won, paying eight dollars; Blarney Stone placed, paying three dollars; and Cinnamon showed, paying five dollars.

senses.definition: To remember where and when (an object or person) has been previously encountered.
senses.example: I've seen him before, but I can't quite place where.

senses.definition: To vouch for someone's alibi.
senses.example: The librarian was placed at home by her neighbor at the time of the murder.

senses.definition: To sing (a note) with the correct pitch.
To make.
senses.example: to place a call

senses.definition: To bet.
senses.example: I placed ten dollars on the Lakers beating the Bulls.

senses.definition: To recruit or match an appropriate person for a job, or a home for an animal for adoption, etc.
senses.example: They phoned hoping to place her in the management team.

senses.definition: To assign (more or less value) to something.
senses.example: My workplace places a high premium on team spirit.

senses.definition: To place-kick (a goal).

core.definition: A particular area, location, or spot where someone or something is, or could be.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the only syllable, and end with a clear voiceless s, not a z. Keep the vowel as a glide from ay toward ee, so avoid flattening it to a short e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word is flexible and carries no emotional charge by itself.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use place for almost any location, including homes, restaurants, cities and workplaces. Saying 'my place' usually means your apartment or house, and 'Let's go to your place' is a natural, casual invitation. In the sense of a spot or position, the word is very common in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Location is more precise and often technical, as in 'GPS location'. Place is the everyday word for the spot where something is.
Spot is informal and usually small and specific, as in 'a good spot for a picnic'. Place can be a whole city, building, or region.
Site refers to a place used for a particular purpose, such as a construction site or a website. Place is the general word.

examples.everyday: Let's meet at my place after work, and I'll order some pizza.
examples.professional: Let's choose a meeting place near the Austin office so the client team can attend in person.
examples.analytical: Every claim in the argument depends on the place it occupies in the larger chain of reasoning.

nuance.analogy: A place is like a pin on a map: it marks exactly where something sits.
nuance.etymology: From Old French place, from Latin platea, 'broad street', from Greek plateia.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'take place' (to happen) with 'take the place of' (to replace someone).
Saying 'at first place' instead of 'in the first place'.

place.etymology: From Middle English *place*, conflation of Old English *plæċe* (“place, an open space, street”) and Old French *place* (“place, an open space”), both from Latin *platēa* (“plaza, wide street”), from Ancient Greek *πλατεῖα*, shortening of *πλατεῖα ὁδός*…

senses.definition: Synonym of plainsong.
senses.example: The choir spent the morning practicing plainchant for the Easter service at the monastery.

core.definition: Unaccompanied, single-line sung church music, especially Gregorian chant used in Catholic and other liturgies.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PLAIN. Say the ch as in 'church' and keep the vowel in chant short, like the a in 'hand'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized musical and religious term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say plainsong or Gregorian chant, and plainchant is used mainly by musicians, church choir directors, and musicologists. You are most likely to hear it in a choir rehearsal, a music history class, or a discussion of liturgy. It does not refer to ordinary speech or conversation.

distinctions.note: Plainsong is a synonym of plainchant, and it is the term more common in English-speaking church music.
Gregorian chant is a specific repertoire of plainchant associated with the Roman Catholic liturgy, so it is narrower than plainchant.
A chorale is a Lutheran congregational hymn with a regular rhythm, and it differs from the free rhythm of plainchant.

examples.everyday: My cousin sings in a choir that does plainchant, and she says it is harder than it sounds.
examples.professional: The music director programmed plainchant for Holy Week and asked the choir to rehearse the modes carefully.
examples.analytical: Plainchant's unison melody and free rhythm shaped how medieval theologians understood the relation between text and sound.

nuance.analogy: Like one clear voice reading a poem aloud, with no harmony or instruments added.
nuance.etymology: Plain comes from Old French plain; chant comes from Old French chant, from Latin cantus (song).
common_mistakes: Stressing chant instead of PLAIN in American speech.
Assuming plainchant is a type of everyday speech or a simple hymn with harmony.

traditions.view: Chanted worship is central to Orthodox services, but Byzantine chant follows its own system of eight modes and is usually not called plainchant.
Gregorian chant is the traditional chant of the Roman rite, sung without instrumental accompaniment, and it is a central part of the liturgy.
Most Protestant churches prefer congregational hymns with harmony and instruments, although Lutherans and Anglicans have kept some chant in worship.

senses.definition: The act or process of overlaying with plaster.
senses.example: The plastering of the nursery walls took two days because the old lath was cracked.

senses.definition: A covering of plaster.

core.definition: The work of covering walls or ceilings with plaster, or the layer of plaster that results.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a quick, unstressed r-colored vowel, not a full 'tar', and the final -ing is short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a trade process and carries no feeling beyond practical description.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'plastering' is mostly a trade word for coating surfaces with plaster, and it appears in construction, renovation and home-improvement talk. Homeowners often discuss 'the plastering' when talking about cost or schedule, and they may say 'plaster work' as well. The uncountable noun is most common, so say 'the plastering was messy' rather than 'a plastering'.

distinctions.note: 'Plaster' is also the material and the verb for applying it, while 'plastering' names the process or the finished coat.
Stucco is a cement-based exterior coating common in the Southwest, while plastering is the general process for interiors and exteriors.
A skim coat is a thin final layer over a wall, while plastering can refer to the full process including the base coat.

examples.everyday: The plastering in our basement took two days, and the walls look great now.
examples.professional: We budgeted two weeks for the plastering, and the schedule depends on drying time between coats.
examples.analytical: Plastering is a process in which wet material is applied and then shaped, so its quality depends on preparation as much as on the final coat.

nuance.analogy: Like icing a cake, plastering smooths a rough surface so that the paint has something even to sit on.
nuance.etymology: From plaster (verb), from Latin emplastrum; the -ing form names the process.
common_mistakes: Using 'a plastering' as a countable noun for one wall, when the noun is usually uncountable
Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full 'tar' instead of a weak r-colored vowel
Confusing it with 'plasticizing' or 'plastic' in construction talk

senses.definition: Enjoying play; sportive; prone to playing frequently, in the manner of a child or young pet (viz. puppy or kitten).
senses.example: Actually, we are pretty playful in our romantic life.

senses.definition: Funny; humorous; jesty; frolicsome; frisky.
senses.example: John is a playful fellow.

senses.definition: Fun; recreational; unserious.
senses.example: A brainteaser is a playful puzzle posed as a test of intelligence.

senses.definition: Experimental.
senses.example: He was a rather playful artist.

core.definition: Full of fun and lighthearted energy; liking to play, joke, or tease, like a child or a young animal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PLAY. The final -ful is usually a syllabic L with no separate vowel, so say it as one soft sound, not 'PLAY-fuh-ul'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes lighthearted, friendly fun. It can also mean someone is joking when a situation is serious, so context matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use playful for people, pets, moods, and remarks, as in 'a playful puppy' or 'a playful tone.' Calling an adult playful is a compliment in most settings. In serious meetings, 'playful' can make a remark sound unserious, so say 'lighthearted' if you mean it as a gentle joke.

distinctions.note: Playful describes a mood or manner of enjoying fun; funny describes something that makes people laugh.
Playful is usually warm and admiring; childish is often negative, implying immaturity.

examples.everyday: My daughter gets really playful when she sees the dog, and they run around the yard for an hour.
examples.professional: I like a playful tone in our team chat, but let's keep the client emails more serious.
examples.analytical: Huizinga argued that play is a playful activity that is free and sets its own rules, which separates it from ordinary life.

nuance.analogy: A playful kitten batting at a string is focused on fun, not on catching anything.
nuance.etymology: From play (Old English plega) plus the suffix -ful, 'full of.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'PLAY-foo-ul' with an extra syllable.
Using playful for a serious situation where you mean 'casual' or 'unofficial.'

senses.definition: In a pleasant manner; so as to achieve a pleasant result.
senses.example: He smiled pleasantly at passersby.

senses.definition: Lightly.
senses.example: The batter was pleasantly light, so the pancakes came out fluffy.

core.definition: In a friendly, agreeable way, or in a way that feels nice and comfortable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PLEH. Say the middle as unt, then end with a light lee sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests a mild, comfortable tone or a happy surprise.
nuance.usage_note: Pleasantly is common in everyday American speech, especially in pleasantly surprised or pleasantly warm. Americans use it to describe how someone greets you, responds or behaves in a calm, friendly manner. It is a soft, polite word rather than an enthusiastic one.

distinctions.note: Happily suggests joy or willingly doing something, while pleasantly suggests a mild, agreeable quality.
Nicely is more informal and everyday; pleasantly is a little more polite and descriptive.

examples.everyday: The weather was pleasantly cool for a July afternoon.
examples.professional: The client responded pleasantly to our revised timeline, which made the call easier.
examples.analytical: The argument is pleasantly straightforward, though it leaves its central premise untested.

nuance.analogy: Pleasantly is like a cool drink on a hot day: it does not thrill you, but it feels good.
nuance.etymology: From pleasant with the suffix -ly, forming an adverb.
common_mistakes: Using pleasantly where pleasingly is meant, as in 'a pleasantly design' instead of 'a pleasing design'.
Saying PLAY-zant-lee instead of PLEH-zunt-lee.

senses.definition: Having or showing pluck, courage or spirit in trying circumstances.
senses.example: Despite the broken leg, the plucky little dog kept chasing the ball across the yard.

core.definition: Showing courage, determination and spirit in a difficult situation, especially when the person or team is weaker.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable with a short 'u' as in 'cup'. The final '-y' is a light 'ee' sound, and the 'ck' is one hard 'k'.

nuance.connotation: Positive, though it can sound slightly patronizing when used for a small or weak underdog, such as 'a plucky little team'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'plucky' in news reports, sports coverage and descriptions of underdogs. It is more common in British English, so in American speech it can sound a little literary or old-fashioned. Describing someone as 'plucky' is a compliment, but calling a larger person or team plucky may sound odd.

distinctions.note: Brave is a general word for facing danger or fear, while plucky emphasizes spirit and determination in a difficult, often underdog, situation.
Gutsy is informal American slang for bold and courageous, sometimes with a sense of risk-taking, and it is more casual than plucky.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor's kid is plucky, even after losing five games in a row.
examples.professional: The startup's plucky team kept shipping features despite losing its budget.
examples.analytical: The author presents the protagonist as plucky, but her courage is more tested than triumphant.

nuance.analogy: A plucky person is like a small sailboat that holds its course through a storm, because it is light and quick but refuses to turn back.
nuance.etymology: From pluck (courage), which originally meant pulling or plucking.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'plucky' with 'lucky', which means having good fortune.
Using 'plucky' to describe a large, powerful person, where it sounds condescending.

senses.definition: Very extravagant. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: They moved into a plush penthouse with gold fixtures and a view of Central Park.

senses.definition: Having a soft, fluffy exterior (of a man-made object, especially stuffed animals or upholstery).
senses.example: This plush toy is so cute and soft — I want it!

senses.definition: A textile fabric with a nap or shag on one side, longer and softer than the nap of velvet.
senses.example: The upholstery was made of a deep green plush that felt soft under my hand.

senses.definition: A plush toy.
senses.example: My daughter carries a worn plush bear everywhere she goes.

senses.definition: To give a soft, fluffy surface to.
senses.example: Before the photo shoot, the stylist plushed the pillows so they looked full and inviting.

core.definition: Soft, thick and luxurious; very comfortable and expensive in look or feel, such as carpets, furniture or hotels.

pronunciation.tip: It rhymes with 'rush' and 'brush'. Make a clear 'sh' at the end and do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive, suggesting comfort and quality. It can be slightly negative if the setting seems too showy or excessive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use 'plush' for hotels, sofas, carpets and velvet, and for 'plush toys' or stuffed animals. In a casual conversation, you might say 'The hotel was so plush'. It sounds friendly and vivid, not formal. When talking about money or power, 'plush' can suggest excess, as in 'a plush office'.

distinctions.note: 'Fluffy' describes something light and airy in texture, while 'plush' suggests a rich, dense softness that also looks expensive.
'Luxurious' is a broader word for anything very expensive or comfortable, while 'plush' focuses on soft, thick textures in furnishings and fabrics.

examples.everyday: We stayed in a hotel with plush carpets and huge white towels, which felt like a real treat.
examples.professional: The client wanted the lobby to feel plush, so the designers chose velvet chairs and dark wood.
examples.analytical: The essay reads the plush interiors of the new banks as signs of a wealth that no longer needs to explain itself.

nuance.analogy: Plush is like sinking into a thick velvet armchair: it feels soft and rich, not just fluffy.
nuance.etymology: From French peluche, from Latin pilus, 'hair'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'plush-ee', which turns it into the different word 'plushie' or 'plushy'.
Using 'plush' for light, fluffy things like a cloud or a pillow, where 'fluffy' fits better.

senses.definition: Synonym of poetical justice (“the idea that in a literary work such as a poem, virtue should be rewarded and vice punished”).
senses.example: The novel's happy ending gave the virtuous heroine her reward, a clear case of poetic justice.

senses.definition: The fact of someone experiencing what they deserve for their actions, especially when this happens in an ironic manner.
senses.example: He cheated his business partners for years, so his arrest felt like poetic justice to everyone.

core.definition: A fitting outcome in which someone gets the punishment or reward they deserve, often in an ironic way.

pronunciation.tip: Keep the main stress on ET in poetic and on JUS in justice. The final 'ice' is pronounced 'iss,' so say JUS-tis, not JUS-teese.

nuance.connotation: Positive for the person who sees it, often satisfying or amusing. It is sometimes used with a touch of irony or schadenfreude.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in casual talk when someone gets a fitting consequence, such as a driver who gets towed while parking illegally. In literature, the phrase describes a fitting end for a character. A natural reply is 'Ha, poetic justice,' or 'Serves him right.' It is not an official legal term, so use it in conversation rather than in court.

distinctions.note: Karma is a spiritual idea of cosmic cause and effect, while poetic justice is a more worldly, often ironic outcome you can see.
Just deserts means a deserved reward or punishment without the ironic twist that poetic justice implies.
Irony is a general figure of speech about opposite meanings; poetic justice is a specific case of an ironic fitting outcome.

examples.everyday: He got a parking ticket right in front of the spot he stole from me, so that's poetic justice.
examples.professional: The vendor who missed every deadline was dropped from the contract, which felt like poetic justice to the whole team.
examples.analytical: In the tragedy, the villain is undone by the very schemes he designed, a form of poetic justice that the play's moral order seems to require.

nuance.analogy: Like a boomerang that comes back to the thrower, the consequence returns to the person who sent it out.
nuance.etymology: Poetic comes from Greek poiētikos, creative; justice comes from Latin iustitia, from ius, right.
common_mistakes: Using poetic justice for any fair outcome, when it implies an ironic or fitting twist.
Stressing the first word of poetic incorrectly as POH-et-ik.
Using it in formal legal writing, where it sounds informal.

poetic-justice.etymology: From *poetic* + *justice*, a variant of *poetical justice*, ( – 1713) in the work The Tragedies of the Last Age Consider’d and Examin’d (1678): see the quotation.

senses.definition: Related to argument or controversy; containing polemic, being polemic.
senses.example: Her polemical essay on immigration drew angry responses from both parties.

senses.definition: Being an attempt to evaluate the arguments comprehensively.
senses.example: The professor's polemical survey weighed every argument for and against the theory.

senses.definition: Prone to causing disputes; inclined to causing the expression of opposing opinions, disputatious, contentious, edgy.
senses.example: The polemical senator loved nothing more than a fight during committee hearings.

senses.definition: A diatribe or polemic.
senses.example: His column was a furious polemical that attacked the mayor's entire budget.

core.definition: Strongly arguing against an opinion or position; intended to attack or dispute rather than to explain neutrally.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LEM. The last two syllables are reduced, so say 'kul' quickly rather than 'kal' or 'kahl.'

nuance.connotation: Mostly negative or neutral. It describes writing or speech that is combative, though it can also praise a text for being forceful and clear.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use polemical mainly to describe articles, books, sermons, or speeches that take a strong side in a dispute. In everyday talk they would more often say argumentative, heated, or one-sided. It is common in academic and religious writing.

distinctions.note: Argumentative describes a person who likes to argue; polemical describes a text or speech that attacks a position in writing or formal debate.
Controversial means the subject provokes disagreement; polemical means the treatment itself is combative and partisan.

examples.everyday: The talk show got so polemical that nobody could finish a sentence without someone shouting.
examples.professional: Let's keep the design review factual, since that memo was too polemical to persuade anyone on the team.
examples.analytical: Although the book is polemical in tone, its critique of the sources is carefully documented and deserves serious engagement.

nuance.analogy: A polemical text is like a courtroom prosecutor's closing statement: it is built to win, not to be neutral.
nuance.etymology: From Greek polemikos, 'warlike,' from polemos, 'war.'
common_mistakes: Confusing polemical with political; polemical means combative in argument, not related to government.
Using polemical as a noun for a person; use polemicist for a person who writes polemics.

senses.definition: Synonym of environmentally friendly.
senses.example: The city council voted to require pollution-free buses by 2030.

core.definition: Containing no pollutants, or produced and operated in a way that does not harm the environment.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound, the strongest stress falls on FREE, and pollution keeps a lighter secondary stress. Say 'free' with a long e and do not reduce it to a weak vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. The phrase is used in marketing and policy to reassure buyers and voters, though it can overpromise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pollution-free on product labels, energy plans and vehicle advertisements, but in technical or policy writing they often prefer zero-emission or low-emission. Because almost every system has some environmental cost, a careful speaker might add 'at the point of use' or say 'cleaner' instead. Note the hyphen when it comes before a noun.

distinctions.note: Environmentally friendly is broader and vaguer, covering resource use and waste as well, while pollution-free claims a specific absence of pollutants.
Zero-emission is a narrower technical term meaning no direct emissions at the point of use, such as an electric car, so it is more precise than pollution-free.

examples.everyday: We bought an electric grill because the company says it's pollution-free, so we can use it on the apartment balcony.
examples.professional: Our new data center runs on pollution-free wind power, which helps us meet the company's emissions targets for next year.
examples.analytical: The phrase pollution-free is rarely literal, because every energy system carries some environmental cost somewhere in its life cycle.

nuance.analogy: Calling something pollution-free is like calling a meal sugar-free: it names one thing that is absent, not a claim that the whole meal is perfect.
nuance.etymology: English compound of pollution (from Latin polluere, 'to defile') and free (from Old English freo).
common_mistakes: Writing pollution free without a hyphen before a noun, as in 'pollution-free air.'
Assuming it means impact-free; it means free of pollutants, which is narrower.

senses.definition: (of a molecule or ion) Consisting of two or more atoms.

core.definition: Of a molecule or ion: consisting of two or more atoms bonded together.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on TAH, in the -tom- syllable, with a light secondary stress on the first syllable. The a in atomic is the ah vowel, not the ay in 'ate.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise scientific term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use polyatomic mainly in chemistry, chemical engineering and science education, as in 'polyatomic ion' for sulfate or nitrate. It contrasts with diatomic, which means exactly two atoms. In everyday conversation it is rarely used outside science.

distinctions.note: Diatomic means exactly two atoms, such as O2 or N2, while polyatomic means two or more, including three or more atoms.
Monatomic means one atom, as in noble gases such as neon or helium, so it is the opposite case.

examples.everyday: My son's chemistry homework asked whether sulfate is a polyatomic ion, so I had to look it up.
examples.professional: The model needs parameters for each polyatomic species, so we should include water and ozone in the reaction set.
examples.analytical: A polyatomic molecule has more vibrational modes than a diatomic molecule, which changes its heat capacity and its spectrum.

nuance.analogy: A polyatomic ion is like a small crew of atoms that moves through solution together, carrying one charge as a single unit.
nuance.etymology: From poly- (Greek polys, 'many') plus atomic, from Greek atomos, 'indivisible.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in POL-ee-uh-tom-ik, instead of pah-lee-uh-TAH-mik.
Using polyatomic for an ion made of a single atom; the word always means more than one atom.

senses.definition: Resembling or characteristic of pork.
senses.example: The sausage had a porky flavor, a bit too fatty and rich for my taste.

senses.definition: Rather fat; chubby.
Singulative of pork (“law enforcement”)
senses.example: Hey, slow down, there's a porky sitting behind that billboard on the highway.

senses.definition: A porcupine.
senses.example: A porky waddled across the trail, quills bristling, as we hiked the ridge.

core.definition: Rather fat or chubby, especially used in an informal or teasing way about a person or animal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, POR. The r is rhotic, and the final y is pronounced as a long ee sound. Do not make the second syllable a separate hard k with a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Negative and mildly insulting when used about a person. It is often said about children or pets with affection, but it can hurt.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use porky in casual speech, often about someone who has gained weight or about a chubby child or pet. Because it can sound rude, use gentler words like chubby or a little heavy in front of the person. The noun sense, singular of pork meaning police, is slang and dated.

distinctions.note: Chubby is usually affectionate about babies and children, while porky can sound more critical about adults.
Stout is a polite, formal word for solidly built, so it is safer in professional or respectful talk.
Obese is a medical term for a serious health condition, not a casual description of looks.

examples.everyday: My brother got a little porky after the holidays, but he's back on his running schedule now.
examples.professional: The budget proposal is a bit porky, so let's trim the extra line items before it goes to the board.
examples.analytical: The essay criticizes the porky bill, which packs unrelated favors into one appropriations package.

nuance.analogy: Porky is like a teddy bear that is not quite soft: it describes a round, heavy shape, often with a teasing tone.
nuance.etymology: From pork, meaning the meat of a pig, plus the suffix -y, meaning having the quality of.
common_mistakes: Using porky in front of the person as a compliment; it can sound insulting.
Confusing porky with porcine, which is a more formal and technical adjective.

senses.definition: In a positive manner.
senses.example: He approached the interview positively.

senses.definition: With certainty.
senses.example: I will positively be there at 8 a.m.

senses.definition: Absolutely; utterly.
Very.
senses.example: I had a positively wonderful time.

core.definition: In a hopeful or favorable way; or, informally, absolutely or certainly, used to add emphasis.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, reduce the middle vowels, and end with a short 'lee' sound. The 't' is often flapped, so it sounds closer to a soft 'd'.

nuance.connotation: Positive when used for hope or approval; in informal intensifier use, it is enthusiastic and emphatic.
nuance.usage_note: In casual speech, Americans use 'positively' as an intensifier, as in 'That was positively delicious,' though 'absolutely' or 'definitely' are more common. It sounds a bit theatrical in everyday talk, so it is best used when you want to add enthusiasm. When someone asks if you are sure, a natural reply is 'Positively, yes' or the simpler 'Absolutely.'

distinctions.note: Absolutely is the everyday American intensifier and answer, while positively sounds more emphatic or dramatic.
Certainly stresses that something is sure, while positively adds strong emphasis or enthusiasm.
Definitely is the more common casual American word for 'for sure', while positively is stronger and less frequent in speech.

examples.everyday: Oh, that new café downtown is positively charming, you have to try it.
examples.professional: The launch metrics responded positively to the new pricing, so we'll keep it.
examples.analytical: The model's coefficient is positively associated with income, meaning higher income predicts higher spending.

nuance.analogy: Positively works like a volume knob on your opinion, turning up the enthusiasm or the favorable tone.
nuance.etymology: From positive plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'positively' as an adjective, as in 'a positively person'; say 'a positive person'.
Using 'positively' where 'definitely' or 'absolutely' would sound more natural in casual American speech.

senses.definition: To hang (a notice) in a conspicuous manner for general review.
senses.example: Post no bills.

senses.definition: To announce publicly; to publish.
senses.example: The company posted record profits this quarter.

senses.definition: To hold up to public blame or reproach; to advertise opprobriously; to denounce by public proclamation.
senses.example: to post someone for cowardice

senses.definition: To carry (an account) from the journal to the ledger.
To inform; to give the news to; to make acquainted with the details of a subject; often with up.
To deposit a payment that may or may not be returned.
senses.example: Since Jim was new to the game, he had to post $4 in order to receive a hand.

senses.definition: To pay (a stake or blind).
senses.example: Since Jim was new to the game, he had to post $4 in order to receive a hand.

senses.definition: To travel with relays of horses; to travel by post horses, originally as a courier.
To travel quickly; to hurry.
To rise and sink in the saddle, in accordance with the motion of the horse, especially in trotting.
To publish (a message) to a newsgroup, forum, blog, etc.
senses.example: I couldn't figure it out, so I posted a question on the mailing list.

senses.definition: To enter (a name) on a list, as for service, promotion, etc.
To assign to a station; to set; to place.
senses.example: Post a sentinel in front of the door.

senses.definition: To pay bail.
senses.example: to post bail

senses.definition: A long dowel or plank protruding from the ground; a fencepost; a lightpost.
senses.example: ram a post into the ground

senses.definition: A pole erected to mark a spot.
senses.example: The posts mark the boundaries of the property.

senses.definition: The stakes that mark the beginning or end of a horse race.
A stud; a two-by-four.
The wire-like core of metal in an earring.
A pole in a battery.
The vertical part of a crochet stitch.
A military base; the place at which a soldier or a body of troops is stationed; also, the troops at such a station.
An organization for delivering letters, parcels etc. or the service provided by such an organization.
senses.example: I sent a parcel via/by post.

senses.definition: A single delivery of letters; the letters or deliveries that make up a single batch delivered to one person or one address.
A message posted in an electronic or Internet forum, or on a blog, etc.

A moderate to deep passing route in which a receiver runs 10-20 yards from the line of scrimmage straight down the field, then cuts toward the middle of the field (towards the facing goalposts) at a 45-degree angle.
senses.example: Two of the receivers ran post patterns.

senses.definition: An assigned station; a guard post.
An appointed position in an organization, job.
Post-production.
senses.example: We'll fix it in post.

senses.definition: A post mortem (an investigation of a body's cause of death).
A goalpost.
A long, narrow piece inserted into a root canal to provide retention for a crown.
A prolonged final melody note, among moving harmony notes.
A printing paper size measuring 19.25 inches x 15.5 inches.
(dated) A station, or one of a series of stations, established for the refreshment and accommodation of travelers on some recognized route.
senses.example: a stage or railway post
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (historical) Someone who travels express along a set route carrying letters and dispatches; a courier.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: With the post, on post-horses; by a relay of horses (changing at every staging-post); hence, express, with speed, quickly.
Sent via the postal service.
Synonym of after, particularly used with historical dating.
senses.example: The chronicle mentions the defenestration of the local bishop, indicating a composition sometime post 1327.

core.definition: To put a message, photo, or comment on a website or social media so other people can see it.

pronunciation.tip: Use the diphthong oh-oo as one smooth vowel, and end with a crisp 'st' cluster. Do not add a vowel between s and t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be positive, as in sharing good news, or negative when someone posts something embarrassing or hostile.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use post for sharing on social media, such as posting a photo or posting an update. For sending something by postal mail, Americans say mail rather than post, which is more common in British English. When someone posts something unkind, people may say they posted about it or called them out.

distinctions.note: Share means sending or passing on someone else's content; post means putting up your own new content for others to see.
Upload is sending a file to a server; post is publishing something on a feed or page, often with text.

examples.everyday: Did you see that I posted a picture of our dinner last night?
examples.professional: Please post the release notes in the team channel before Friday's standup.
examples.analytical: When a public figure posts a statement online, the message is shaped by the platform's norms and the expectation of immediate, widespread replies.

nuance.analogy: Posting is like pinning a note to a community bulletin board where anyone who walks by can read it.
nuance.etymology: From Old French poste and Latin positus, 'placed'; the online sense developed in the late 20th century.
common_mistakes: Using post to mean mail a letter, which Americans usually say as 'mail it'.
Confusing post as a verb about social media with post as a noun for a pole or a job.

post.etymology: Middle English *post*, from Old English *post* (“pillar, door-post”) and Old French *post* (“post, upright beam”), both from Latin *postis* (“door, post, doorpost”).

conversation.text: Did you see what she posted on Instagram?
I posted the pictures from the beach.
They posted a sign saying the pool is closed.

senses.definition: Any animal or other organism that hunts and kills other nonplant organisms (their prey), primarily for food.
Someone who attacks and plunders for gain.
senses.example: The corporate raider was a predator who bought struggling companies only to strip their assets.

senses.definition: A sexual predator.
senses.example: Police warned parents about a known predator hanging around the playground.

core.definition: An animal that hunts and kills other animals for food; also a person who exploits others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PRED-. The final syllable is a weak 'ur' sound, and the middle 'uh' is often nearly silent in quick speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative when describing a person who exploits or harms others; neutral when describing animals in nature.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'predator' for lions, hawks and other hunters in nature, and for people who take advantage of others, such as scam artists or 'predatory' lenders. When speaking about sexual crimes, 'predator' is a common but serious term, so use it carefully. In everyday talk, people often say 'hunter' for animals.

distinctions.note: 'Prey' is the animal that gets hunted; 'predator' is the one that hunts.
'Hunter' can be a neutral or sporting term; 'predator' emphasizes the animal's role as a natural killer or a person's exploitative behavior.

examples.everyday: Be careful at the campsite; there are coyotes around, and they're natural predators of small pets.
examples.professional: The fraud team flagged a predator account that was targeting new users with fake refund offers.
examples.analytical: Hobbes describes a state of nature in which every person is a predator toward others, which he sees as a reason for a social contract.

nuance.analogy: A hawk over a field: its whole life is built around spotting and catching what moves below.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praedator, 'plunderer, hunter', from praedari 'to plunder'.
common_mistakes: Using 'predator' only for animals; in English it also refers to people who exploit others, so context matters.
Saying 'PRED-a-tor' with a clear 'ah' vowel in the second syllable; the middle vowel is reduced.

predator.etymology: Latin *praedātor*, from *praedor* (“loot, pillage”), from *praeda* (“booty, spoils, prey”).

senses.definition: To show or suggest ahead of time; to represent beforehand.
senses.example: The early sketches seemed to prefigure the sweeping curves of the final building.

senses.definition: To predict or foresee.
senses.example: Nobody could have prefigured the market crash that followed the housing boom.

senses.definition: That which prefigures or appears to predict; a harbinger.

core.definition: Something that prefigures or appears to predict a later event or thing; a harbinger or early sign.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, FIG. The noun and verb share the same pronunciation, so only the grammar changes.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an early sign or symbol without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use prefigure as a noun; it is mostly a verb in modern English. In formal or literary writing a noun use may appear, but people more often say 'harbinger', 'sign' or 'foreshadowing'. Use the noun only if you are sure it reads naturally in context.

distinctions.note: Harbinger is the common noun for an early sign of something to come; prefigure as a noun is rarer and more literary.
An omen is often seen as a supernatural sign, while a prefigure is a symbolic or foreshadowing representation.

examples.everyday: The first warm day in March was a prefigure of the spring we had been waiting for.
examples.professional: The beta release was a prefigure of the full product, showing the team what users would ask for.
examples.analytical: For the author, the sacrifice in the story is a prefigure of a greater redemption that the book only hints at.

nuance.analogy: A prefigure is like the first swallow in spring, a sign that the season is about to change.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praefigurare, from prae 'before' and figurare 'to form, shape'.
common_mistakes: Treating prefigure as the common noun; people normally say harbinger or sign in everyday English.
Using the noun and verb with different stress; both are pronounced pree-FIG-yer.

prefigure.etymology: From Middle English *prefiguren*, from Latin *praefigurare*, from *figurare* (“to shape, picture”).

senses.definition: The state or quality of being primitive.
senses.example: The museum's exhibit on early tools highlighted the primitivism of life in the Stone Age.

senses.definition: The opinion that life was better or more moral among primitive peoples, or among children, and has deteriorated with civilization.
senses.example: Her essay on primitivism argued that modern people had lost something that tribal societies still possessed.

senses.definition: Any of a group of related styles in the arts, influenced by a belief in the superiority of primitive forms.
senses.example: The gallery's show of early twentieth-century works captured the primitivism of Gauguin's Tahitian paintings.

core.definition: The belief that simple or early peoples, or children, are morally superior to civilized adults; also an early 20th-century art movement drawing on folk and non-Western forms.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PRIM, and the -ism ending is a reduced uh sound. Say the middle vowels quickly, with the t in primitive as a light t, not a flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in art history; in philosophy, it can be positive about simplicity or negative when it romanticizes others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use primitivism mainly in art history, philosophy, and cultural criticism. It names both a romantic idea that civilization corrupts people and a modernist style. Because the term can be used critically, speakers often add context such as 'romantic primitivism' or 'modernist primitivism'.

distinctions.note: Primitiveness describes a quality of things; primitivism names a doctrine or artistic movement that values that quality.
Naturalism represents nature or ordinary life realistically; primitivism idealizes simple or early forms, often as a rejection of civilization.

examples.everyday: My art teacher is really into primitivism, so she loves paintings that look childlike and rough.
examples.professional: The gallery's curator framed the exhibit around primitivism, showing how modern painters borrowed from African and Oceanic forms.
examples.analytical: Primitivism rests on the assumption that civilization corrupts human nature, an idea that reverses the Enlightenment narrative of progress.

nuance.analogy: Like nostalgia for a childhood home: an idealized picture of a simpler past that the present is said to have lost.
nuance.etymology: From primitive, from Latin primitivus, 'first of its kind', from primus, 'first', with the suffix -ism, meaning 'doctrine or practice'.
common_mistakes: Using primitivism for a plain quality; for the quality itself, use primitiveness.
Assuming the word is always positive; in cultural criticism, it often means an idealization that can be condescending.

senses.definition: Synonym of stochastic process.

core.definition: A random process whose outcomes change over time according to probabilities rather than fixed rules; another name for a stochastic process.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress in 'probabilistic' falls on 'lis', not on 'pro', so say 'prah-buh-bih-LIS-tik'. Pronounce 'process' with stress on the first syllable and no extra vowel at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It describes a mathematical model without any evaluative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in mathematics, statistics, engineering, and data science when modeling systems that evolve randomly over time. The phrase is often shortened to stochastic process in papers, but probabilistic process is common in teaching and applied work. It is not a casual phrase, so you would use it in a meeting about a model or a lecture rather than in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: The two phrases mean the same thing; stochastic is the more common term in research papers, while probabilistic process is common in teaching and applied work.
A random variable is a single quantity with a probability distribution, while a process is a whole family of random variables indexed by time.
A deterministic process has no randomness, so the same starting state always gives the same result.

examples.everyday: Stock prices bounce around in a way that looks like a probabilistic process, which is why nobody can predict them exactly.
examples.professional: We described user arrivals as a probabilistic process indexed by time, so the capacity plan reflects the natural variability of traffic.
examples.analytical: A probabilistic process is a family of random variables indexed by time, and its future behavior depends on how its past states constrain it.

nuance.analogy: A probabilistic process is like a river flowing through a valley: you know its general direction, but each drop's exact path depends on chance.
nuance.etymology: Probabilistic comes from probability, from Latin probabilitas; process comes from Latin processus, meaning progress or course.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'PRO' in probabilistic, as in 'PRAH-buh-bil-IS-tik' instead of the correct 'prah-buh-bih-LIS-tik'.
Using probabilistic process to mean a process that is merely uncertain in everyday life; in technical use it means a formal model of random evolution over time.

senses.definition: A distribution of all possible values of a random variable together with an indication of their probabilities.

core.definition: A function listing all possible values of a random variable together with the probability of each value.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'BIL' in 'probability' and 'BYOO' in 'distribution'. The 'tr' in distribution sounds like 'chr' in fast speech, and the final 'tion' is 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in statistics, machine learning and data science courses and work. Speakers often shorten it to 'distribution' when the context is clear, such as 'the normal distribution'. It is rarely used in everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: A probability distribution often refers to the whole spread of probabilities, while a density function describes continuous variables specifically.
A frequency distribution counts observed data, while a probability distribution describes what is expected in theory.

examples.everyday: My coworker explained that a probability distribution shows all the possible outcomes and how likely each one is.
examples.professional: Before we choose a model, we should check which probability distribution best fits the customer wait times.
examples.analytical: A probability distribution encodes a theory of uncertainty, so its assumptions about the shape of the tail can shape conclusions.

nuance.analogy: A probability distribution is like a map of hills and valleys over possible outcomes: the high points are the most likely results.
nuance.etymology: Probability from Latin probabilitas; distribution from Latin distributio, 'division, arrangement'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable in 'distribution', as in 'dis-trib-YOO-shun'.
Confusing a probability distribution with a sample of data; the distribution is the theoretical model.

conversation.text: A language model outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next token.
We assumed a normal probability distribution for the errors, but the residuals have heavy tails.

senses.definition: The mathematical study of probability (the likelihood of occurrence of random events in order to predict the behavior of defined systems).
senses.example: She studied probability theory before applying statistical models to predict customer churn.

core.definition: The branch of mathematics that uses axioms to study random events and calculate how likely outcomes are.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'BIL' in probability and the first syllable of 'theory', pronounced with a long e as in 'thee'. Do not shorten the 'ee' to 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, used to name a field of study.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in mathematics and statistics departments to name the formal theory of random events. It is more specific than probability alone, which can mean a number or a general sense of likelihood. In everyday speech Americans just say probability or odds.

distinctions.note: Probability theory deduces consequences from a known model, while statistics infers the model from observed data.
Probability is a number or a measure of likelihood, while probability theory is the whole mathematical field that studies it.
Decision theory uses probability to choose actions under uncertainty, while probability theory focuses on the mathematics of chance itself.

examples.everyday: I took a probability theory class in college, and it still helps me judge the odds when I make decisions.
examples.professional: Before we run the A/B test, let's review the probability theory behind the confidence intervals so everyone agrees on the assumptions.
examples.analytical: Probability theory, built on Kolmogorov's axioms, supplies the logical structure within which statistical inference becomes meaningful.

nuance.analogy: Probability theory is like the grammar of chance: it does not tell you what will happen, but it gives the rules for reasoning correctly about what might happen.
nuance.etymology: Probability comes from Latin probabilitas, and theory comes from Greek theōria, meaning contemplation or speculation.
common_mistakes: Using probability theory to mean a single probability estimate for one event.
Pronouncing 'theory' with a short i as in 'THIH-ree' instead of the American 'THEER-ee'.

senses.definition: Likely or most likely to be true.
senses.example: It's probable that it will rain tomorrow.

senses.definition: Likely to happen.
senses.example: With all the support we have, success is looking probable.

senses.definition: Supporting, or giving ground for, belief, but not demonstrating.
senses.example: The detective's evidence made her guilt probable, though it was not yet proven.

senses.definition: Something that is likely.
senses.example: Given the forecast, a rain delay is the probable, so we should prepare.

senses.definition: A person who is likely to appear or do a certain thing.
senses.example: Coach named three probables for the team, and the rest are still fighting for spots.

core.definition: Likely to be true or to happen, based on the evidence available, though not certain.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second and third syllables are reduced to a quick schwa, so it sounds like two syllables, PRAH-bl. Avoid pronouncing the middle syllable as a full 'bay' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it expresses a reasoned estimate of likelihood rather than a hope or a fear.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'probable' in everyday talk, often as 'It's probable that...' or 'That's probable,' though 'likely' is more common in casual speech. In professional and academic writing it is standard for stating a judgment about likelihood. Saying 'probably' as a reply is more natural in conversation than 'probable.'

distinctions.note: 'Likely' is more common and more conversational; 'probable' sounds slightly more formal or technical.
'Possible' means it could happen at all; 'probable' means it is more likely than not.
'Plausible' describes an explanation that seems believable; 'probable' describes how likely something actually is.

examples.everyday: It's probable that the store will be closed on Monday, so let's go on Sunday.
examples.professional: Given the drop in traffic, it is probable that the campaign underperformed in March.
examples.analytical: The hypothesis is probable given the evidence, though it is not yet demonstrated.

nuance.analogy: Like a forecast of seventy percent rain: you expect it, but you still bring an umbrella.
nuance.etymology: From Latin probabilis, 'worthy of approval, credible,' from probare, 'to test, prove.'
common_mistakes: Using 'probable' as an adverb; say 'probably' ('He will probably come').
Pronouncing the final syllables as full vowels instead of reduced ones.

probable.etymology: From Middle English *probable*, from Old French *probable*, from Latin *probābilis* (“that may be proved, credible”), from *probāre* (“to test, examine”); see *probe*, *probity*, *prove*.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or characteristic of a professor or professors, or of a professorship or professorships.

core.definition: Relating to a professor, or having the scholarly, formal manner often associated with professors.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on SOR, with a weaker secondary stress on PRO. The middle syllables are weak, and the -ial ending is pronounced ee-uhl.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It can praise scholarly authority but often implies pedantry or stiffness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use professorial to describe a manner or appearance, such as a professorial tone, air or glasses. It rarely describes a professor's job; for that, people say academic or faculty. The word often carries light humor or mild criticism.

distinctions.note: Scholarly praises learning and research, while professorial describes a style or manner, often with a hint of formality or stiffness.
Academic describes the university world or theoretical work, while professorial describes how someone speaks or looks.

examples.everyday: He gave a long, professorial explanation of why you should always salt pasta water.
examples.professional: Her professorial style works well in a lecture hall, but it feels stiff in a daily team stand-up.
examples.analytical: The essay adopts a professorial tone that assumes the reader already accepts its premises.

nuance.analogy: A professorial manner is like a well-worn tweed jacket: it signals expertise, but it can feel out of place at a backyard barbecue.
nuance.etymology: From professor plus the adjective suffix -ial.
common_mistakes: Stressing PRO instead of SOR, as in pro-fuh-SOR-ee-uhl.
Using professorial to mean academic for a research topic; it describes a manner, not a subject.

senses.definition: To make Protestant; to convert to Protestantism.
To become Protestant; to convert to Protestantism.

core.definition: To make someone or something Protestant, or to convert a person or community to Protestantism.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TES, the second syllable. The 'ant' is reduced to a weak 'un' sound, so it sounds like 'tun' in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in historical writing, but can sound pointed or polemical when used by someone critical of Protestantism.
nuance.usage_note: This word is rare and appears mainly in church history, theology, and scholarly writing about the Reformation or mission work. In ordinary American speech, people would say 'convert to Protestantism' or 'become Protestant' instead. Because it can sound pointed, use it carefully when discussing religious communities with people who hold different beliefs.

distinctions.note: Convert is the everyday word for changing religion, while Protestantize is more formal and often describes changing an institution or practice rather than one person.
Reform means to improve or change a system, while Protestantize specifically means shaping something to fit Protestant belief or practice.

examples.everyday: My grandmother said the mission had tried to Protestantize the village, but people kept their old feast days anyway.
examples.professional: In the seminar, the lecturer argued that the reformers did not simply Protestantize medieval parishes; they reshaped them.
examples.analytical: Historians debate whether the rulers used the edicts to Protestantize their territories or merely to allow confessional choice.

nuance.analogy: To Protestantize a church is like repainting an old house in a new style: the walls stay in place, but the look and purpose change.
nuance.etymology: From Protestant plus the verb suffix -ize.
common_mistakes: Using it as a synonym for 'become religious,' when it specifically refers to Protestant belief or practice.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in pruh-tes-TAN-tyz, instead of pruh-TES-tun-tyz.

senses.definition: The act of protruding.
senses.example: The slow protrusion of the drill bit through the wall alarmed the crew.

senses.definition: The state of being protruded.
senses.example: A reduction in growth was accompanied by protrusion of the calyx.

senses.definition: Anything that protrudes.
senses.example: A rocky protrusion jutted from the cliff, forming a natural lookout above the valley.

core.definition: Something that sticks out from a surface, or the act of sticking out; a bump, ledge or projection.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TROO, the second syllable. The ending -sion is pronounced 'zhun', like 'vision', not 'shun' as in 'action'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a physical shape without judgment, though in medicine it can signal a concern.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'protrusion' in medicine (a disc protrusion), engineering, and formal descriptions. In everyday speech, people say 'bump', 'lump', 'ledge', or 'sticking-out part'. A doctor may say 'protrusion' when describing a bulging spinal disc.

distinctions.note: A bump is informal and usually small; a protrusion can be larger and is more precise, often technical.
A bulge suggests a swelling outward from the middle of a surface, while a protrusion is any part that sticks out past the surface.

collocations: a metal protrusion on the wall

examples.everyday: There's a little metal protrusion on the back of the door that keeps catching my coat.
examples.professional: The design review flagged a protrusion on the housing that interferes with the cable routing.
examples.analytical: Descartes treats the body as an extended thing, and the protrusion of a limb is simply one more arrangement of matter in space.

nuance.analogy: A protrusion is like a shelf bracket sticking out from a wall, the part that catches your eye as you walk past.
nuance.etymology: From Latin protrusio, from protrudere, 'to thrust forward'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as 'shun' instead of 'zhun'.
Using protrusion for an emotional or social sense, such as 'a protrusion of personality', which sounds odd.

senses.definition: A service performed for the public good.
senses.example: They feel that public service is a noble calling that calls for every citizen in one way or another.

senses.definition: A service such as health care, transport, or waste removal provided to the general public, often by the government.
The organization, department or business providing such a service.
Government employment, especially in the civil service.
senses.example: After college, she took a job in public service with the state housing agency.

core.definition: A service such as transit, water or fire protection provided to all members of the public, usually by government; also work done for the common good.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SUR, the r-colored vowel in 'service'. The final syllable is a weak 'us' like the end of 'bus', with no 'ice' sound, and the t in public is silent.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests dedication and selflessness, especially in government and nonprofit contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use public service for government work such as teaching in a public school, working as a firefighter, or holding a city job, and they call the people public servants. The phrase also names services like buses or the water supply. In everyday talk, people might say 'I work in public service' or simply 'I work for the city'.

distinctions.note: Civil service refers to government employees and the system that hires them, while public service is broader and includes volunteering or any work for the community.
Customer service is help given to paying customers by a business, while public service is provided to the community, often free or subsidized.

examples.everyday: My cousin has worked in public service for ten years, mostly at the city water department.
examples.professional: The project team will track how many residents use each public service after the new transit route opens.
examples.analytical: A healthy democracy depends on citizens who see public service as a responsibility rather than just a career ladder.

nuance.analogy: Public service is like a shared kitchen in an apartment building: everyone depends on it and helps maintain it for the common good.
nuance.etymology: Public from Latin publicus; service from Latin servitium, from servus, 'slave, servant'.
common_mistakes: Confusing public service with customer service, which is a business's help for paying customers
Pronouncing service with a long i, as in SUR-vice

senses.definition: A young dog, wolf, fox, seal, bat or shark, or the young of certain other animals.
senses.example: The dog has had that bed since he was just a pup.

senses.definition: A young, inexperienced person.
senses.example: The new teacher is a mere pup.

senses.definition: Any cute dog, regardless of age.
senses.example: My pup likes to run as fast as he can, yet cannot always stop in time!

senses.definition: A short semi-trailer used jointly with a dolly and another semi-trailer to create a twin trailer.
senses.example: The freight company hauled two pups behind the tractor on the interstate.

senses.definition: A new plant growing from a shoot that can be used for propagation.
senses.example: Cut the pup from the base of the pineapple and root it in water.

senses.definition: A kind of small spotlight.
senses.example: The film crew set up a pup on the stage to light the actor's face.

senses.definition: An early edition of a periodical publication, intended for distribution to distant locations.
senses.example: The newsroom printed a pup of the magazine for readers overseas.

senses.definition: Someone who participates in pup play (the sexual practice of role-playing as a young dog).
senses.example: At the kink conference, a pup and handler shared tips on safe role-play.

senses.definition: A small tributary or feeder stream in the US state of Alaska.
senses.example: We pitched our tent beside the pup where it feeds into the Chena River.

senses.definition: To give birth to pups.
senses.example: The seal pupped on the rocky shore during the early spring.

core.definition: A young dog, or a young animal such as a seal, wolf, fox, or shark; also an informal word for a young, inexperienced person.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short u of 'cup' and end with a clean, unreleased 'p'. Do not add a vowel after the p.

nuance.connotation: Affectionate for animals. Calling a person 'a pup' is mildly condescending, suggesting they are young and green.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'pup' casually for a young dog or for baby seals, pups, and foxes; in formal writing, 'puppy' is used for dogs. Calling a coworker 'just a pup' is informal and slightly patronizing. The verb 'to pup' is technical and used mainly for animals giving birth.

distinctions.note: Puppy is the standard word for a young dog; pup is shorter and used more widely for young animals of many kinds.
Whelp is literary and can be a slightly insulting term for a young person or animal; pup is more casual.

examples.everyday: Look at that little pup trying to catch the ball, he's so cute!
examples.professional: The new analyst is still a pup, so pair him with someone senior until he gets the hang of the reporting tools.
examples.analytical: The author describes the pups in the den as dependent beings whose survival shapes the pack's entire social order.

nuance.analogy: A pup is a dog still learning the rules of the house, just as a new hire is still learning the rules of the office.
nuance.etymology: Short for 'puppy', which comes from Middle French 'poupée', meaning doll.
common_mistakes: Calling an adult dog a 'pup'; the word refers to a young animal.
Using 'pup' for a young person in formal settings, where it sounds dismissive.

put-all-your-eggs-in-one-basket.phonetic: /ˌpʊt ˌɔl jɔɹ ˌɛɡz ɪn ˌwʌn ˈbæskət/

senses.definition: Do not dedicate all your resources to one project.
senses.example: Don't put all your eggs in one basket; diversify your savings across stocks, bonds, and cash.

senses.definition: Do not count on any one thing to safeguard what is valuable.
senses.example: I back up my thesis twice because I never put all my eggs in one basket.

core.definition: To risk everything on a single option, plan, or investment, so that a single failure could cause a total loss.

pronunciation.respelling: put awl yor eggz in wun BAS-kit
pronunciation.tip: In natural speech 'all your' blends into 'awl-yer' and 'in one' sounds like 'in-wun', and the main stress lands on BAS in 'basket'. Americans often say 'basket' with a clear 't' sound in a quick, flapped form as 'BAS-kit'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to cautionary; it is a piece of advice warning against risk concentration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom in business, finance, career, and personal decisions, often as advice like 'Don't put all your eggs in one basket by relying on one client.' It can be said casually to friends or in a meeting. A natural reply is 'Good point, let's diversify', or 'You're right, we should have a backup plan'.

distinctions.note: Hedge your bets means to protect yourself by supporting more than one outcome; put all your eggs in one basket names the mistake of not doing so.
A backup plan is a concrete alternative; the idiom is a general warning about risk.

collocations: don't put all your eggs in one basket
put all your eggs in one basket
avoid putting all your eggs in one basket
keep your eggs in different baskets

examples.everyday: My uncle says don't put all your eggs in one basket, so I kept some savings in a separate account.
examples.professional: We should not put all our eggs in one basket by relying on a single cloud vendor for the whole pipeline.
examples.analytical: The argument is an application of diversification: a portfolio that places all its eggs in one basket is exposed to correlated failure.

nuance.analogy: Putting all your eggs in one basket is like carrying every dish you own on one tray, so if you trip, everything breaks at once.
common_mistakes: Using 'put your eggs in one basket' without 'all', which weakens the expression.
Saying 'in the one basket' with an article; the idiom is usually 'in one basket'.

conversation.text: Don't put all your eggs in one basket; apply to more than one school.
We shouldn't put all our eggs in one basket with one big client.
Investing everything in one stock is putting all your eggs in one basket.

senses.definition: To fester or rot and exude a fetid stench.
senses.example: Left in the summer heat, the fish began to putrefy within hours and smelled awful.

senses.definition: To become filled with a pus-like or bile-like substance.
senses.example: The infected wound began to putrefy, filling with yellowish pus that needed draining.

senses.definition: To reach an advanced stage of decomposition.
senses.example: Three weeks in the woods, the deer carcass had begun to putrefy beyond recognition.

senses.definition: To become gangrenous.
senses.example: Without antibiotics, the soldier's infected leg would soon putrefy and require amputation.

senses.definition: To make morbid, carious, or gangrenous.
senses.example: to putrefy an ulcer or wound

senses.definition: To corrupt; to make foul.
senses.example: Greed can putrefy even the most idealistic movements from within.

core.definition: To rot and decay, giving off a foul smell, as dead flesh or food does when left to spoil.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PYOO. Reduce the middle syllable to a quick uh, and keep the t light, almost like a d, before the r.

nuance.connotation: Negative. The word suggests disgusting decay and foul smell, so it is rarely used for neutral or pleasant change.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use putrefy mostly in scientific, medical, or literary writing about dead matter. In everyday talk they say rot, go bad, or spoil. Saying something 'putrefied' at a dinner table would sound stiff and over-dramatic.

distinctions.note: Rot is everyday and common; putrefy is more formal and stresses the foul smell and gases of decomposition.
Decay is broader and can describe teeth, buildings, or reputations; putrefy is limited to organic matter that stinks.
Spoil is the normal word for food going bad in a kitchen; putrefy is stronger and suits more advanced decay.

examples.everyday: Throw out that chicken before it starts to putrefy in the fridge.
examples.professional: The lab report said the tissue samples began to putrefy because the cooler failed during shipping.
examples.analytical: Medieval preachers often described the sinful soul as one that putrefies from within, drawing on older Christian language about corruption.

nuance.analogy: Like a fruit left in a warm room, a thing that putrefies goes from fresh to rotten and stinks as it breaks down.
nuance.etymology: From Latin putrefacere, from puter (rotten) and facere (to make).
common_mistakes: Using putrefy for any kind of change; it refers only to foul decay of organic matter.
Stressing the second syllable; say PYOO-truh-fy, not puh-TREF-y.

senses.definition: In a rash manner; hastily or without due consideration; with precipitation.
senses.example: She rashly accepted the offer without reading the contract or asking any questions.

core.definition: In a hasty way, without thinking carefully about the consequences.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final '-ly' is a light 'lee' sound, and the 'sh' sound stays crisp.

nuance.connotation: Negative, implying careless or unwise action.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rashly mainly in writing, formal speech, or serious discussion of decisions and promises. In casual talk they usually say too quickly or without thinking. It often appears in news, legal, and religious contexts.

distinctions.note: Hastily describes speed alone, while rashly adds the idea of poor judgment.
Recklessly stresses disregard for danger, while rashly stresses a lack of thought.

examples.everyday: Don't rashly agree to the trip before you check your schedule.
examples.professional: We should not rashly change the database schema without testing the migration.
examples.analytical: The text warns that those who speak rashly before God risk regretting their words.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver who speeds through a yellow light without looking, rashly acting skips the moment of checking.
nuance.etymology: From rash (adjective) plus the adverbial ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using rashly for speed alone; it always implies poor judgment
Placing it between the verb and object in a way that sounds awkward; say decide rashly rather than rashly decide when stress matters
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the idea of acting rashly is tied to speaking or vowing without thought before God. The Hebrew word mahar means to hurry or be quick, and it appears in warnings against hasty speech and hasty vows. Ecclesiastes 5:2 warns against being rash with the mouth and hasty of heart before God. Proverbs 19:2 warns that making haste with the feet can lead one astray, a picture of acting without reflection. Acts 19:36 counsels the crowd in Ephesus not to do anything rash, showing the word in a civic setting.

senses.definition: The deduction of inferences or interpretations from premises, abstract thought, ratiocination; any instance of this, especially as a process leading to an action, motive.
senses.example: Her reasoning was clear and logical.

senses.definition: A Rastafari meeting held for the purposes of chanting, prayer and discussion.
senses.example: On Saturday night the community gathered for reasoning, drumming, and prayer at the yard.

core.definition: The process of thinking logically from facts, premises, or evidence to reach a conclusion or decision.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, REE. The final -ing has a short ih vowel, so say 'REE-zun-ing,' not 'REE-zun-eeng.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. Good reasoning is admired, while faulty reasoning is criticized.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'reasoning' often in everyday talk, as in 'I don't follow your reasoning' or 'That's faulty reasoning.' It can also mean the explanation behind a decision, as in 'The reasoning behind the change is that costs went up.' In Rastafari communities in Jamaica, 'reasoning' can also name a gathering for discussion, chanting, and prayer.

distinctions.note: Logic is the formal study of valid inference, while reasoning is the everyday process of drawing conclusions.
An argument is a set of reasons presented to persuade someone, while reasoning is the thinking process behind it.

examples.everyday: I get your point, but your reasoning about the car repair doesn't add up to me.
examples.professional: Please walk us through your reasoning before we approve the model's threshold for fraud alerts.
examples.analytical: Kant's transcendental reasoning begins from the conditions of possible experience rather than from empirical generalizations.

nuance.analogy: Like a bridge built one plank at a time, each step resting on the one before.
nuance.etymology: From reason (verb) with the suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'reasoning' with 'reason.' Reasoning is the thinking process, while reason is the cause or justification.
Saying 'reasonings' as a plural in everyday English. It is more natural to say 'lines of reasoning' or 'different reasoning.'

senses.definition: A language model trained to work through problems step by step before answering.
senses.example: The reasoning model paused to check each step of the proof before giving its final answer.

core.definition: An AI language model trained to work through a problem in steps, checking its logic, before giving an answer.
